- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates downside risk; add downward buffer or adjust for volatility clustering.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overcorrects and overshoots; apply dampening factor or reduce forecast growth rate.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa), model lags in adjusting; prioritize sentiment-driven reversion or momentum reversal signals.
- In low-sentiment periods, model tends to forecast mean-reversion too aggressively; avoid forcing sharp downward moves unless sentiment confirms.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion after a spike, model often fails to recognize it; use sentiment + price history to trigger early correction.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often overestimates upward trend in bullish sentiment; cap forecast at 1.5x recent high if sentiment > 0.7.
- If sentiment is consistently low (0.00) and price is trending down, model may underestimate depth; add 5–10% downward adjustment for extreme bearish sentiment.
